page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E6.Flex.64-256 is a compute-oriented virtual machine instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It is driven by an AMD EPYC 9J45 processor operating at a base clock speed of 2.7 GHz. The instance configuration allocates 64 dedicated physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled, supplying 128 virtual CPUs alongside 256 GB of system RAM.

The hardware configuration establishes a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, allocating exactly 2.0 GB of memory per logical thread. The instance includes no local storage or discrete GPU hardware, meaning persistent storage must be provisioned via attached network block volumes. Network configuration includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. The resource layout targets CPU-bound workloads where memory density is secondary to parallel processing capability.

From a cost efficiency standpoint, the dedicated physical allocation ensures predictable performance without the noisy-neighbor tradeoffs of shared-core systems. The instance is suited for multi-threaded compilation tasks, continuous integration and continuous deployment pipelines, scientific batch processing, and horizontally scaled application tiers that demand high parallel CPU throughput without substantial in-memory capacity.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E6.Flex.64-256 is an x86_64 compute-oriented virtual machine powered by an AMD EPYC 9J45 processor clocked at 2.7 GHz. It allocates 64 dedicated physical cores with two threads per core, yielding 128 vCPUs alongside 256 GB of system memory. Operating at a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio with 2.0 GB per thread, the instance emphasizes dense thread parallelism over large memory footprints. No local storage drives or discrete GPUs are bundled, necessitating external block storage for non-volatile persistence. With one complimentary public IPv4 address provided, this instance delivers consistent dedicated CPU capacity for multi-threaded batch operations, high-throughput CI/CD compilation workloads, mathematical modeling, and distributed microservices where raw processing capacity is prioritized over local disk caching or expansive memory arrays.
